## Coordinates for the Paulis {#sec-paulis}

Finite groups are among the simplest objects in mathematics, and among
the most quietly powerful. A group is a finite collection of things with
a single operation that combines any two of them into a third. The rule
that gives the idea its force is closure: combine two members and you
land on a member again, every time, so you can go on combining forever
without ever leaving the set or enlarging it. The smallest example worth
naming is a group of just two elements,
$$
\mathbb{Z}_2 = \{0, 1\},
$$
combined by addition modulo two:
$$
0 + 0 = 0, \qquad 0 + 1 = 1, \qquad 1 + 1 = 0.
$$
A light switch, a coin turned over and over: two states and one move that
flips between them, with nowhere else to go. That last rule, $1 + 1 = 0$,
is the XOR sitting inside every one-bit adder.

Groups get far richer than counting modulo something, and one question
sorts them more sharply than any other: does the order of combining
matter? Take two members, combine them one way, then the other way
round, and you may or may not land in the same place. In $\mathbb{Z}_2$
you always do, and a group where that always holds is called
*commutative*, or in the usual group-theoretic word, *abelian*. Keep the
question in view. The operators this post is heading toward will answer
it with a no, and that refusal to commute is the seam the whole argument
runs along.

What we need from a group here is not a classification, though. It is a
way to make one concrete enough to work with, so that it can be aimed at
our original question about dividing the depolarizing channel. That
bridge is a *representation*: attach a matrix to each element so that
multiplying the matrices reproduces the group's own operation, carrying
an abstract group over into concrete linear algebra. For $\mathbb{Z}_2$
it can be as small as two $2 \times 2$ matrices,
$$
0 \;\longmapsto\; \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
1 \;\longmapsto\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
The first does nothing; the second swaps the two entries it acts on, a
flip. Multiply the flip by itself and the swaps cancel, returning the
identity, exactly as $1 + 1 = 0$ in the group. Before reading on, it is
worth confirming for yourself that this really is a representation: it
has to turn every sum in the group into the matching product of
matrices. There are only four sums to check, so run the identity and the
flip through all of them and watch each one land on the nose. Addition
modulo two has become matrix multiplication, and that translation is so
fruitful that the representation theory of finite groups is a deep and
thoroughly mapped field in its own right.

We built $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and its representation as a rehearsal, because
the qubit is one honest step up from it. Read $\mathbb{Z}_2$ as the
arithmetic of a single classical bit: one coordinate over $\{0, 1\}$,
the only move being to flip it or leave it, and the representation we
just built was the pair $\{I, \text{flip}\}$. One coordinate, no phase.
That is the whole classical system.

Now let us be bold and simply widen it. Give the group a second
coordinate, change nothing else, and see what we are forced into. The
group is
$$
\mathbb{Z}_2^2 = \bigl\{ (0,0),\; (1,0),\; (0,1),\; (1,1) \bigr\},
$$
four labels added entry by entry modulo two, and we go hunting for a
representation of it by $2 \times 2$ matrices exactly as before.

Two of the four assignments are already settled. The label $(0,0)$ does
nothing, so it takes the identity, and the first coordinate is still the
classical flip, so $(1,0)$ takes the flip matrix. The second coordinate
is the genuinely new one, and the simplest move a qubit has that a bit
does not is a *sign*: leave both levels in place, but flip the sign of
the second. That is $(0,1)$. The last label $(1,1)$ means both at once,
and the matrix that does both, fixed up so that it names an axis of the
Bloch ball like the other three, completes the set:
$$
(0,0) \;\longmapsto\; I, \qquad
(1,0) \;\longmapsto\; X, \qquad
(0,1) \;\longmapsto\; Z, \qquad
(1,1) \;\longmapsto\; Y,
$$
with
$$
I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
X = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
Y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
Z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
These are the *Pauli matrices*, and they are not strangers. They are the
$x$, $y$, $z$ axes of the Bloch ball we have been drawing all along,
with the identity sitting at the centre. Write $\sigma(\eta)$ for the
matrix this map attaches to the label $\eta$, so that $\sigma(0,0) = I$
and $\sigma(1,0) = X$; that shorthand carries the rest of the chapter.
Read a label $(a, b)$ as two yes-or-no questions, $a$ for "does it
flip?" and $b$ for "does it pick up a sign?", and this two-coordinate
space, the classical bit widened by a phase axis, is the qubit's *phase
space*.

So far the widening has cost us nothing. Now make it earn its keep and
check that the map really is a representation, the way you checked the
two-element case. Every sum of labels has to come out as the matching
product of matrices. Plenty of the checks pass without complaint:
$(1,0) + (1,0) = (0,0)$ on the label side, and $X^2 = I$ on the matrix
side.

Then take $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. The labels add to $(1,1)$, which the map
sends to $Y$. Multiply the two matrices in that order, though, and
$$
XZ \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; -i\,Y.
$$
Close, but not equal. A factor of $-i$ has appeared out of nowhere, and
the labels have nowhere to record it.

It gets worse, and the way it gets worse is the whole point. Multiply
the same two matrices in the opposite order:
$$
ZX \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; +i\,Y,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad XZ = -ZX.
$$
And there is the answer to the question we left hanging. Addition in
$\mathbb{Z}_2^2$ is commutative, so $(1,0) + (0,1)$ and $(0,1) + (1,0)$
are the very same label: the labels are blind to the order you worked
in. The matrices are not. They come out differing by a sign.

That is fatal to the strict goal, and no cleverer choice of the four
matrices rescues it. The labels commute, the operators do not, and
rescaling the assignments only shuffles the phases around without ever
removing them.

```{=html}
<details class="aside">
<summary>Why no choice of phases can repair it</summary>
```

Suppose we tried to patch the mismatch by rescaling the assignment,
replacing $\sigma(\eta)$ by $\sigma'(\eta) = c_\eta\,\sigma(\eta)$ for
some nonzero numbers $c_\eta$.
Whenever two labels commute, which in $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$ is always, a
genuine representation would need
$\sigma'(\eta)\,\sigma'(\xi) = \sigma'(\xi)\,\sigma'(\eta)$. But
$$
\sigma'(\eta)\,\sigma'(\xi) = c_\eta c_\xi\,\sigma(\eta)\,\sigma(\xi), \qquad
\sigma'(\xi)\,\sigma'(\eta) = c_\xi c_\eta\,\sigma(\xi)\,\sigma(\eta),
$$
and $c_\eta c_\xi = c_\xi c_\eta$, because ordinary numbers commute. The
two sides therefore still differ by exactly the factor that
$\sigma(\eta)\,\sigma(\xi)$ and $\sigma(\xi)\,\sigma(\eta)$ differed by in the first
place, which for $X$ and $Z$ is $-1$. Rescaling moves the phases about;
it cannot remove them.

```{=html}
</details>
```

The failure is an interesting one, though, and worth naming precisely.
Adding labels records *which* operator you land on and quietly loses the
phase you gathered getting there. So the Paulis are not a representation
of $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$ in the strict sense we set up for $\mathbb{Z}_2$.
They are a representation *up to a phase*, a *projective* one. The
classical bit had nothing of the sort; the new coordinate arrived with a
phase riding on top of it.

That phase is the one genuinely new ingredient the quantum problem hands
us, and naming it well is most of the work ahead. Carry it as a function
sitting on top of the phase space, a single phase pinned to each vector.
Then anything built from these operators, a channel included, comes apart
into two clean pieces: a rule that moves the phase-space vectors around,
and this phase function riding along above them. Those two pieces, and
nothing heavier, are all we need to take the qubit apart.

### Narrowing the field

Time to make good on that promise, and to bring back the question the
post is actually about.

Recall what we are after. The completely depolarising channel $P$ erases
every input in a single step, and we want to write it as $P = S^k$ for a
channel $S$ that takes as many identical steps as possible to do the
same damage. For a qubit we already know the ceiling. Any such $S$ acts
nilpotently on the three traceless directions, so $k \le 3$. What we do
not know is whether anything reaches it.

Hunting through the full space of channels is unpleasant work. Even for
one qubit a channel carries a Choi matrix with on the order of $d^4$
free numbers in it, and the condition that picks out the physically
allowed ones, complete positivity, is not a list of separate bounds on
those numbers but a single global positivity requirement. Tracking where
it holds as the entries vary is delicate here and hopeless higher up. We
would rather not confront that space head-on.

So let us cut it down, and the Bloch ball shows where to cut. A unital
channel is pinned down entirely by what it does to the three coordinate
axes, and those axes are $X$, $Y$ and $Z$. A general channel may send
each one wherever it pleases: the image of $X$ can tilt off into a blend
of all three, the ball is squashed into a skewed ellipsoid, and the
three clean axes end up smeared into one another. That freedom is
precisely what we just called hard to oversee.

Here is the restriction, and it is a severe one. Demand that each Pauli
be carried to a single Pauli, at most rescaled, never to a mixture of
them. Geometrically the ellipsoid is no longer allowed to tumble: its
principal axes stay aligned with the originals, permuted among
themselves and stretched or squeezed, but never rotated into off-axis
directions. The rule already has a pedigree. The unitaries that send
Paulis to Paulis under conjugation are exactly the *Clifford group*, the
well-behaved gates at the heart of quantum error correction. The maps we
have just described are their dissipative relatives: same
Paulis-to-Paulis bookkeeping, but allowed to *shrink* an axis rather
than merely permute it, and it is in that shrinking that forgetting will
live. We call them *Clifford channels*.

::: {#fig-clifford-grid}

{{< include figures/fig5-continuum-grid/interactive.qmd >}}

Left: the qubit state space, a continuum that a general channel can
deform into an ellipsoid at any angle. Right: the four labels $(a, b)$,
with $a$ counting bit-flips and $b$ phase-flips, so $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$,
$(1,1)$ are the $X$, $Z$, $Y$ axes and $(0,0)$ is the identity. A
Clifford channel may stretch or swap the three coloured axes but never
tilt them, so all of its "where each direction goes" freedom is the map
$h$ permuting these finitely many points. The origin $(0,0)$, the
identity every copier fixes, stays put; for the qubit, $h$ is just a
permutation of the other three.

:::

Written out, a Clifford channel does exactly this:
$$
T[\sigma(\eta)] = \lambda(\eta)\,\sigma(h(\eta)).
$$
There are the two pieces we were promised, and there is nothing else in
it. The first is the relabelling $h$, the rule that moves the labels
around. Because multiplying Paulis adds their labels, $h$ has to respect
that addition, and that pins it down: it must be an invertible linear
map of the plane $\mathbb{Z}_2^2$ fixing the origin. For the qubit there
are only $3! = 6$ of them, the permutations of the three nonzero labels.
The second piece is $\lambda$, the phase function riding above, now one
number per label giving the factor by which that axis is stretched or
shrunk. This is where forgetting lives. An amplitude below one in
magnitude damps an axis, and an amplitude equal to zero erases it
outright.

Two facts make this a sensible place to hunt. The target is already in
the class, since $P$ fixes the identity and annihilates every other
Pauli, which is the Clifford form with trivial $h$ and every amplitude
but the central one set to zero. And the class is closed under
composition: feed one Clifford channel into another and the relabellings
compose while the amplitudes multiply. The whole equation $S^k = P$
plays out inside the class, so taking roots never throws us back into
the wilderness.

### Iterating is now bookkeeping

Apply $T$ twice and watch. The output of the first application is itself
a single Pauli, so $T$ knows exactly what to do with it:
$$
T^2[\sigma(\eta)] = \lambda(\eta)\,T[\sigma(h(\eta))]
= \lambda(\eta)\,\lambda(h(\eta))\,\sigma(h^2(\eta)).
$$
Apply it $n$ times and the pattern is plain:
$$
T^n[\sigma(\eta)] = \Biggl(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda\bigl(h^j(\eta)\bigr)\Biggr)\,\sigma\bigl(h^n(\eta)\bigr).
$$

Sit with that for a moment, because the fog has lifted completely.
Iterating the channel did two clean and separate things. The label
moved, a single point hopping around the plane under repeated
application of the one matrix $h$. And an amplitude piled up, a running
product, one factor collected at each label the point lands on. That
sequence of labels is the *orbit* of $\eta$ under $h$.

Now recall what $P$ does. It leaves the identity alone and annihilates
everything else. The identity takes care of itself, since
$\lambda(0) = 1$ for any channel that preserves the trace. So asking for
$T^k = P$ is asking for the accumulated amplitude to vanish on every
nonzero label after exactly $k$ steps:
$$
\prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \lambda\bigl(h^j(\eta)\bigr) = 0
\qquad \text{for every } \eta \neq 0.
$$
A product of numbers is zero exactly when one of its factors is. So the
condition says something you can picture: travelling along the orbit of
any nonzero label, the point has to step on a label where $\lambda$
vanishes within the first $k$ moves. Push $k$ as high as it will go
while still erasing every orbit, and you have the longest root.

Let me state it with no quantum mechanics in the sentence at all. We
want a point that, started anywhere nonzero and moved repeatedly by $h$,
takes as long as possible to first land on a marked square.

### The qubit answer

For a qubit the plane holds four points and the origin sits the game
out, so everything comes down to three labels,
$$
(1,0) = X, \qquad (0,1) = Z, \qquad (1,1) = Y,
$$
and to how long a permutation of them can postpone the inevitable.

Take $h$ as long as it goes. The best available is a three-cycle, for
instance
$$
h = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\qquad \text{over } \mathbb{F}_2,
$$
which sends $X \to Z \to Y \to X$ and fixes the origin. One orbit,
sweeping every nonzero label before returning home.

Now place the zeros of $\lambda$, and here the qubit is handed a gift
worth understanding, because it is the thing that will be taken away
again in the next chapter. Preserving Hermiticity forces a relation
between the amplitude at a label and the amplitude at its mirror image,
$$
\lambda(-\eta) = \overline{\lambda(\eta)},
$$
so the two always have the same size, and a zero at $\eta$ drags a zero
to $-\eta$ with it. At $d = 2$ the arithmetic is modulo two, so
$-\eta = \eta$ and every label is its own mirror. The relation collapses
to $\lambda(\eta) = \overline{\lambda(\eta)}$, which says nothing more
than that the amplitudes are *real*. It forces no second zero anywhere.

So a single zero suffices. Set $\lambda(X) = 0$ and leave the other two
alone, say $\lambda(Y) = \lambda(Z) = \tfrac12$. Follow each label
around the cycle and count how long it survives:

- $X$ is marked, so it dies on the first step.
- $Y$ moves to $X$, so it dies on the second.
- $Z$ moves to $Y$, then to $X$, so it takes all three.

Every nonzero label is gone by step three, and one of them is still
alive after step two. That is exactly $T^3 = P$ with $T^2 \neq P$, so
$$
k = 3 = d^2 - 1 \qquad \text{at } d = 2.
$$

There is the qubit's answer in full. A Clifford channel, carrying
nothing but a permutation of three labels and three real numbers,
divides total erasure into three equal steps, and three is the most that
*any* quantum channel on a qubit can manage. We threw away almost all
the freedom in the space of channels and lost nothing at all. For the
qubit, the Clifford toolbox is already the full toolbox.

You have met this channel before, as it happens. Back in
@fig-bloch-root we drew a maximal qubit root sending a Bloch vector
$(r_1, r_2, r_3)$ to $(r_2/2,\, r_3/2,\, 0)$, with the $x$-axis
collapsing at once and the $z$-pole taking all three steps. That is
precisely the channel we have just built: the vanishing amplitude is
$\lambda(X) = 0$, the two survivors are the halves, and the $z$-pole is
the hero because $Z$ is the label furthest from the mark. The picture
came first. Now the finite plane explains it.
